title: How do you find the cause of a latency regression after a release?
summary: Distinct from live p99 triage during an active incident — a slower, deploy-correlated investigation that bisects across recent changes to find which one is responsible.

slides.markdown:
This is a different problem from debugging a spike you're seeing right now. Here, you already know performance got worse *sometime after a release* — the task is a slower, forensic investigation: compare metrics before and after the deploy boundary, then isolate which of possibly several shipped changes actually caused it.

The interviewer is testing whether you have a systematic bisection process, not "we'd look at the logs around when it happened" — that answer doesn't scale once several unrelated changes shipped together in the same release.

Ask how many changes shipped between the last-known-good period and now — a single deploy makes this almost trivial; a week's worth of changes bundled together makes it a real investigation requiring a bisection strategy.

Ask whether the regression is uniform across all traffic, or isolated to one endpoint or segment. A regression hitting every endpoint equally points toward something shared (infrastructure, a common library); one isolated to a single endpoint points toward a change specific to that code path — which narrows your suspect list dramatically before you even start comparing metrics.

Compare before/after metrics right at the deploy boundary first — did the shift happen exactly at the release, or does the timing not line up cleanly? If it lines up and multiple changes shipped in that window, **bisect**: roll back or feature-flag each change independently and compare the same metric against each variant.

The deploy boundary is your anchor — everything else is narrowing from there. For how this connects to a broader rollout process (and why flagging changes at deploy time is what makes bisection possible later), see [rolling out a design](rolling-out-a-design).

![One endpoint's p99 latency diverging upward right at the deploy marker while others stay flat](assets/percentile-overlay-deploy.svg)

Overlay p50/p95/p99 latency for the 24 hours before and after the deploy, per endpoint. This isolates exactly which endpoint's percentile shifted, and by how much — a diverging p99 on one endpoint while every other stays flat tells you both where to look and roughly how severe the regression is.

This view alone often narrows a system-wide-feeling complaint down to one specific code path before you've bisected anything.

assets.alt: One endpoint's p99 latency diverging upward right at the deploy marker while others stay flat

slides.markdown:
p99 for the search endpoint rose from 180ms to 640ms after a release that bundled three unrelated changes. Feature-flagging each one off independently in a canary shows the new relevance-scoring model — not the two other changes shipped alongside it — is responsible, because it added a synchronous call to a scoring service that wasn't there before.

Without flags, the team would have been staring at three innocent-looking diffs with no way to isolate which one actually mattered — the bisection is only possible because each change could be toggled independently after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: when you can't cleanly bisect
slides.markdown:
If changes were deployed together without feature flags, per-change bisection isn't available after the fact. The fallback: a targeted rollback of the entire release to confirm the regression disappears — that at least confirms the release, not something unrelated, is the cause.

That rollback buys time to bisect properly in a follow-up deploy, this time with each change flagged independently so the next investigation (hopefully never needed) has the tooling this one lacked. Rolling back doesn't identify the specific culprit — it stops the bleeding and defers the precise diagnosis.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Bisecting via feature flags is precise, but only works if changes were flagged at deploy time — a decision made *before* you knew you'd need it.

| Situation | Available approach | Precision |
|---|---|---|
| Changes were flagged at deploy time | Toggle each flag independently, compare metrics | High — isolates the exact change |
| Changes shipped together, unflagged | Coarse full rollback, or a slower forensic trace-level investigation | Lower — confirms the release, not the specific cause |

This is the argument for flagging risky changes before you need this: the investigation you can run later is decided by a choice made at deploy time, not at incident time.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the regression started 2 hours after the deploy
slides.markdown:
Yes, this changes the suspect list — look for something that ramps rather than an instant cause. Three concrete candidates: a cache warming up cold and only becoming a bottleneck once it's fully populated and being evicted under pressure; a gradual traffic ramp (the deploy landed off-peak) exposing an N+1 query that only bites at higher volume; or a resource leak that takes time to accumulate to the point it matters.

An instant-onset regression points at the code itself; a delayed one points at something environmental interacting with the code over time — the investigation strategy shifts accordingly.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: you found the responsible change — roll back or fix forward?
slides.markdown:
Roll back first to stop user impact immediately — the priority once you've identified the cause is restoring service, not proving you understand it perfectly. Then fix the underlying issue and re-deploy, with the fix specifically verified in canary before a full rollout.

Trying to patch a live regression in place, under pressure, risks a second bad deploy stacked on top of the first — rolling back removes the time pressure entirely, letting the actual fix get the same careful, staged rollout as any other change.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming the most visible change is the cause
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The biggest, most obvious change in this release is almost certainly the cause — let's roll that one back."

**Why it's wrong:** without actually isolating the cause via metrics comparison or flag bisection, you're guessing based on visibility, not evidence. Rolling back the wrong change wastes the rollback (the regression persists) and, worse, the real cause ships again unnoticed in the next release since nobody actually found it.

**Correct model:** always confirm via a before/after metrics comparison or flag toggle before acting — "most recent" and "most visible" are weak priors, not evidence, and the search endpoint scenario in this topic is a case where the actual culprit was neither the biggest nor the most obviously risky-looking change.

Anchor on the deploy boundary: compare before/after metrics per endpoint first. If several changes shipped together, bisect by toggling each one independently — this only works if they were feature-flagged at deploy time, which is the real argument for flagging risky changes proactively.

Without flags, fall back to a full rollback to stop the bleeding, then bisect properly in a follow-up deploy. Once you've found the cause, roll back first and fix forward carefully — never patch a live regression under pressure, and never assume the most visible change is the culprit without actually verifying it.
